explanations.explanation: God says to Ezekiel, the prophet, "Son of man, wail for the multitudes of Egypt…" (Ezekiel 32:18). Wailing is a loud, sorrowful cry. I think this is a heavy assignment, friend, and I'd rather sit quietly with it than crack a joke.

I get why this one pulls at you, because a warning feels like the natural next step. But nothing in this message tells Ezekiel, the prophet, to warn anyone to run. God says, "Son of man, wail for the multitudes of Egypt…" (Ezekiel 32:18). The instruction is to wail.

No battle cry anywhere in this one, friend. The word that comes to Ezekiel, the prophet, is "Son of man, wail for the multitudes of Egypt…" (Ezekiel 32:18). That's a sorrowful cry, not a trumpet. The sword does show up in the message, but nobody is told to gather an army.

explanations.answer: To the depths of the earth
explanations.explanation: God tells Ezekiel to "consign her and the daughters of the mighty nations to the depths of the earth with those who descend to the Pit" (Ezekiel 32:18). The Pit is where this whole message is headed. Egypt has company on the way down, and that's the big picture here.

Cush is a real place in the Bible, but it's not named in this message. The text says Egypt and the daughters of the mighty nations go "to the depths of the earth with those who descend to the Pit" (Ezekiel 32:18). This isn't a trip to another country. It's a trip down.

Babylon never appears in these verses, friend. The message sends Egypt and the daughters of the mighty nations "to the depths of the earth with those who descend to the Pit" (Ezekiel 32:18). That's a way down, not a place on a map.
The message says, "Go down and be placed with the uncircumcised!" (Ezekiel 32:19). Notice how often that word comes back in this passage. It's said again and again, and I'd keep an ear out for it.
Israel's kings aren't mentioned in this part. The message says, "Go down and be placed with the uncircumcised!" (Ezekiel 32:19). That's the group named, so that's the group we stay with.

That sounds like it could fit, but the text doesn't say it. It says, "Go down and be placed with the uncircumcised!" (Ezekiel 32:19). When the Bible names the company, we keep to the company it names.
The message says, "Let them drag her away along with all her multitudes." (Ezekiel 32:20). Egypt doesn't go down alone. Her multitudes are right there with her.
The text says the opposite, friend. It reads, "Let them drag her away along with all her multitudes." (Ezekiel 32:20). Her multitudes go with her, so the answer is True.

"Mighty chiefs will speak from the midst of Sheol about Egypt and her allies…" (Ezekiel 32:21). Sheol is the place of the dead. The ones speaking were powerful once, and now they speak from down there. I think it's a sobering picture.
Pharaoh's magicians are not mentioned in this passage. The speakers are "Mighty chiefs" who speak "from the midst of Sheol" (Ezekiel 32:21). Pharaoh himself comes up later in the passage.

Babylon's wise men never take the stage in these verses, friend. The text says, "Mighty chiefs will speak from the midst of Sheol about Egypt and her allies…" (Ezekiel 32:21). Chiefs are the ones doing the talking.

The text says Assyria's company was among "those who once spread terror in the land of the living" (Ezekiel 32:23). Now they lie in the depths of the Pit. It's a heavy picture, friend. That much terror once, and now they're down there.
Temples aren't mentioned here. The text says Assyria's company are "those who once spread terror in the land of the living" (Ezekiel 32:23). That's what the passage remembers about them.

Feeding the poor is a good thing, but it's not what this verse says about Assyria's company. They are "those who once spread terror in the land of the living" (Ezekiel 32:23). Terror is the word that sticks.

Verse 24 says of Elam's multitudes, "They bear their disgrace with those who descend to the Pit." (Ezekiel 32:24). Elam, a nation far to the east, once spread terror in the land of the living. Now disgrace is what they bear.
The text says otherwise, friend. Of Elam's multitudes it says, "They bear their disgrace with those who descend to the Pit." (Ezekiel 32:24). Elam is a nation far to the east. The statement is True.

This one is easy to slide past, since the text says the opposite. Of Meshech and Tubal it says, "They do not lie down with the fallen warriors of old, who went down to Sheol with their weapons of war…" (Ezekiel 32:27). Those warriors had swords under their heads and shields on their bones. Meshech and Tubal aren't lying with them.

The text says, "They do not lie down with the fallen warriors of old, who went down to Sheol with their weapons of war, whose swords were placed under their heads, whose shields rested on their bones…" (Ezekiel 32:27). Meshech and Tubal are set apart from them. I'm told you can't see this one coming, so nice work.

Right in the middle of the list, the message turns: "But you too will be shattered and lie down among the uncircumcised, with those slain by the sword." (Ezekiel 32:28). The text doesn't say here who "you" is, so I'm leaving that open too. What it does say is plain. The same end waits there.

explanations.answer: You will be spared this time
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the text offers a pass. The message says, "But you too will be shattered and lie down among the uncircumcised, with those slain by the sword." (Ezekiel 32:28). That little word "too" matters, because it puts "you" with all the others on the list.

explanations.answer: You will rule over them all
explanations.explanation: The text goes the other direction, friend. It says, "But you too will be shattered and lie down among the uncircumcised, with those slain by the sword." (Ezekiel 32:28). Nobody here rules over the others. They all lie down together.

Might didn't buy Edom a way out, friend. The text says her kings and princes, "who despite their might are laid among those slain by the sword" (Ezekiel 32:29). Edom is Israel's neighbor. The statement is False, because they are laid among the slain.

The text says Edom's kings and princes, "who despite their might are laid among those slain by the sword" (Ezekiel 32:29). Their might doesn't keep them out. It's in the verse right there, "despite their might."

The text says, "Pharaoh will see them and be comforted over all his multitude…" (Ezekiel 32:31). Pharaoh is Egypt's king. The verse says he is comforted and doesn't tell us why. So I'll leave that open, and just stay with what it says.
That's a natural guess with all the terror in this passage. But the text says, "Pharaoh will see them and be comforted over all his multitude…" (Ezekiel 32:31). Comforted is the word it gives.

explanations.answer: He will cry out for help
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the verse has Pharaoh crying out. The text says, "Pharaoh will see them and be comforted over all his multitude…" (Ezekiel 32:31). He sees them, and he is comforted.

God has the last word: "For I will spread My terror in the land of the living…" (Ezekiel 32:32). The line has come around the whole passage about other nations, and now it's "My terror." That's a serious ending, friend, and I think it deserves a quiet moment.
Babylon isn't named in the passage, friend. In the last verse, the Lord GOD says, "For I will spread My terror in the land of the living…" (Ezekiel 32:32). The terror in that line is His own.

Earlier verses talk about nations who spread terror, but the last verse changes whose terror it is. The Lord GOD says, "For I will spread My terror in the land of the living…" (Ezekiel 32:32). "My" is the word to catch.
